meta.titre: Propositional Logic: implication, contrapositive and truth tables

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Pure Mathematics with Mechanics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A teacher in Bamenda tells her class: "If you finish the past papers, you will pass." A student who did not finish the papers and still passed has not made the teacher a liar, yet many candidates think the promise was broken. Everyday speech hides the exact meaning of words such as "if", "or" and "not", and a mistake here costs marks. Propositional logic gives each of these words one precise meaning that can be tested in a truth table. At Advanced Level the paper asks you to build truth tables, to write the contrapositive of an implication, and to translate symbols into ordinary English.

items: A statement is a sentence that is definitely true or definitely false, but not both.
The words "and", "or" and "not" are used to join or change statements.
A table with 2 columns of letters can list every combination of two choices, such as heads or tails for two coins.

sections.titre: Connectives, implication, contrapositive and truth tables
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Statements and connectives
A statement is a sentence that is either true (T) or false (F). If $p$ and $q$ are statements, the connectives are: negation $\sim p$ ("not $p$"), conjunction $p\wedge q$ ("$p$ and $q$"), disjunction $p\vee q$ ("$p$ or $q$", where "or" is inclusive: at least one is true), implication $p\Rightarrow q$ ("if $p$ then $q$") and the biconditional $p\Leftrightarrow q$ ("$p$ if and only if $q$"), which is true when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth value.

| $p$ | $q$ | $\sim p$ | $p\wedge q$ | $p\vee q$ | $p\Rightarrow q$ | $p\Leftrightarrow q$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | F | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | F | T | F | F |
| F | T | T | F | T | T | F |
| F | F | T | F | F | T | T |

The implication is false in only one case: $p$ true and $q$ false. When $p$ is false the implication is true whatever $q$ is. In $p\Rightarrow q$, $p$ is the hypothesis and $q$ the conclusion.

### Converse, inverse and contrapositive
From $p\Rightarrow q$ we form three related statements:

| $p$ | $q$ | $p\Rightarrow q$ | $q\Rightarrow p$ | $\sim p\Rightarrow\sim q$ | $\sim q\Rightarrow\sim p$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | T | T | F |
| F | T | T | F | F | T |
| F | F | T | T | T | T |

Columns 3 and 6 are identical, so the contrapositive $\sim q\Rightarrow\sim p$ is equivalent to the original implication. The converse and the inverse are not equivalent to it (they are equivalent to each other). An implication can also be rewritten as $\sim p\vee q$.

### Negations (De Morgan's laws)
$$
\sim(p\wedge q)\equiv(\sim p)\vee(\sim q),\qquad \sim(p\vee q)\equiv(\sim p)\wedge(\sim q) \tag{1}
$$

$$
\sim(p\Rightarrow q)\equiv p\wedge(\sim q) \tag{2}
$$

### Truth tables
With $n$ statements the table has $2^n$ rows, listed systematically (for two statements: TT, TF, FT, FF). Add one column for every sub-expression, working from the innermost brackets outwards, and put the required compound statement in the last column. A compound statement that is true in every row is a tautology, one that is false in every row is a contradiction, and two statements are equivalent when their final columns are identical.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question defines statements $p$ and $q$ in words and asks for a compound statement in ordinary English, or the reverse.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Let $p$: "The market is open" and $q$: "Mary buys rice". Then $p\Rightarrow q$ reads "If the market is open, then Mary buys rice"; $p\wedge q$ reads "The market is open and Mary buys rice"; $\sim p\vee q$ reads "The market is not open or Mary buys rice". To write $\sim q$, negate the verb: "Mary does not buy rice". Always keep the order of the symbols and write complete sentences in the same tense as the given statements.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to prove that two statements mean the same, or that a statement is always true.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Build one table containing both compound statements and compare the two final columns row by row. Identical columns prove equivalence; a final column of T only proves a tautology. State your conclusion in a sentence, for example "The final columns are identical, so the two statements are equivalent."

sections.enonce_markdown:
Two statements are defined as $p$: "Mary studies hard" and $q$: "Mary passes the examination".

(a) Write, in words, the statement $p\Rightarrow q$ and its contrapositive.

(b) Construct a truth table for $r=(p\Rightarrow q)\wedge(\sim q)$ and state a simpler statement that is equivalent to $r$.

etapes.justification: The contrapositive of $p\Rightarrow q$ is $\sim q\Rightarrow\sim p$: negate both statements and reverse them.
etapes.resultat_markdown:
$p\Rightarrow q$: "If Mary studies hard, then she passes the examination."

$\sim q\Rightarrow\sim p$: "If Mary does not pass the examination, then she did not study hard."

etapes.action: List every combination of truth values.
etapes.justification: There are two statements, so the table needs $2^2=4$ rows, written TT, TF, FT, FF.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The rows are TT, TF, FT, FF, as in the first two columns of the table in the next step.

etapes.justification: $p\Rightarrow q$ is false only in the row where $p$ is T and $q$ is F, and $\sim q$ swaps T and F in the $q$ column.
etapes.resultat_markdown:
| $p$ | $q$ | $p\Rightarrow q$ | $\sim q$ | $r=(p\Rightarrow q)\wedge(\sim q)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | F | F |
| T | F | F | T | F |
| F | T | T | F | F |
| F | F | T | T | T |

etapes.justification: A conjunction is true only when both parts are true. Both are true only in the last row ($p$ false, $q$ false), where $p\Rightarrow q$ is T and $\sim q$ is T.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The last column of the table gives F, F, F, T.

etapes.justification: A statement that is true only when $p$ is false and $q$ is false is $\sim p\wedge\sim q$. Compare its column with that of $r$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The final columns of $r$ and $\sim p\wedge\sim q$ are identical, so $(p\Rightarrow q)\wedge(\sim q)\equiv\sim p\wedge\sim q$. In words: $r$ is true exactly when Mary did not study hard and did not pass.

items.erreur_markdown: "$p\Rightarrow q$ is false when $p$ is false, because the condition did not happen."
items.pourquoi_faux: The implication is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false. When $p$ is false, nothing has been broken, so $p\Rightarrow q$ is true whatever $q$ is.
items.correction_markdown: In the table, rows 3 and 4 (where $p$ is F) give T for $p\Rightarrow q$.

items.erreur_markdown: Giving $q\Rightarrow p$ as the contrapositive of $p\Rightarrow q$.
items.pourquoi_faux: $q\Rightarrow p$ is the converse, which is not equivalent to the original (it differs in the row where $p$ is F and $q$ is T). The contrapositive negates both statements and reverses them.
This is not De Morgan's law: for $p$ true and $q$ false, $\sim(p\wedge q)$ is T but $\sim p\wedge\sim q$ is F. The connective must change when the negation passes through the brackets.
items.correction_markdown: $\sim(p\wedge q)\equiv\sim p\vee\sim q$ and $\sim(p\vee q)\equiv\sim p\wedge\sim q$.

items.erreur_markdown: Treating $p\vee q$ as "either $p$ or $q$ but not both", so entering F in the TT row.
items.pourquoi_faux: In logic, $\vee$ is inclusive: $p\vee q$ is true when at least one of $p$, $q$ is true, including when both are.
items.correction_markdown: Enter T in the TT row for $p\vee q$; it is false only in the FF row.

items.erreur_markdown: Drawing a table for two statements with only three rows (TT, TF, FF).
items.pourquoi_faux: Two statements have $2^2=4$ combinations, and the missing row (FT) may be exactly the one that decides whether two statements are equivalent.
items.correction_markdown: List all four rows: TT, TF, FT, FF; for three statements use $2^3=8$ rows.

items.enonce_markdown: Let $p$: "A shape is a square" and $q$: "The shape has four sides". Write in words the converse, the inverse and the contrapositive of $p\Rightarrow q$, and say which of them are equivalent to $p\Rightarrow q$.
items.solution_markdown:
$p\Rightarrow q$: "If a shape is a square, then it has four sides."

Converse $q\Rightarrow p$: "If a shape has four sides, then it is a square."

Inverse $\sim p\Rightarrow\sim q$: "If a shape is not a square, then it does not have four sides."

Contrapositive $\sim q\Rightarrow\sim p$: "If a shape does not have four sides, then it is not a square."

Only the **contrapositive** is equivalent to $p\Rightarrow q$. The converse and the inverse are both false for this pair of statements: a rectangle that is not a square has four sides.

items.enonce_markdown: Construct a truth table for $(p\vee q)\wedge\sim(p\wedge q)$ and describe in words when this statement is true.
items.solution_markdown:
| $p$ | $q$ | $p\vee q$ | $p\wedge q$ | $\sim(p\wedge q)$ | $(p\vee q)\wedge\sim(p\wedge q)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T | F | F |
| T | F | T | F | T | T |
| F | T | T | F | T | T |
| F | F | F | F | T | F |

The final column is F, T, T, F. So the statement is true when **exactly one of $p$ and $q$ is true** (this is the exclusive "or"), and false when both are true or both are false.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Use a truth table to show that $\sim(p\Rightarrow q)$ is equivalent to $p\wedge\sim q$.

(b) Hence write the negation of "If a student attends every lesson, then the student passes" in ordinary English.

(c) Determine whether $(p\Rightarrow q)\vee(q\Rightarrow p)$ is a tautology.
items.solution_markdown:
(a)

| $p$ | $q$ | $p\Rightarrow q$ | $\sim(p\Rightarrow q)$ | $\sim q$ | $p\wedge\sim q$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | F | F | F |
| T | F | F | T | T | T |
| F | T | T | F | F | F |
| F | F | T | F | T | F |

The columns for $\sim(p\Rightarrow q)$ and $p\wedge\sim q$ are identical (F, T, F, F), so they are equivalent.

(b) With $p$: "A student attends every lesson" and $q$: "The student passes", the negation is $p\wedge\sim q$: **"A student attends every lesson and does not pass."**

(c)

| $p$ | $q$ | $p\Rightarrow q$ | $q\Rightarrow p$ | $(p\Rightarrow q)\vee(q\Rightarrow p)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | T | T |
| F | T | T | F | T |
| F | F | T | T | T |

The final column is T, T, T, T, so the statement **is a tautology**.

items_markdown: $p\Rightarrow q$ is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false; $p\vee q$ is inclusive and is false only when both are false.
The contrapositive $\sim q\Rightarrow\sim p$ is equivalent to $p\Rightarrow q$; the converse $q\Rightarrow p$ and the inverse $\sim p\Rightarrow\sim q$ are not (but are equivalent to each other).
De Morgan: $\sim(p\wedge q)\equiv\sim p\vee\sim q$, $\sim(p\vee q)\equiv\sim p\wedge\sim q$, and $\sim(p\Rightarrow q)\equiv p\wedge\sim q$.
A truth table has $2^n$ rows; work from the inner brackets outwards, one column per sub-expression, final statement last.
Equivalent statements have identical final columns; a tautology has only T in its final column.
